Infectious disease · published research

Osteomyelitis

One small sham-controlled pilot found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated foot ulcers, and a very small jaw study reported better postoperative healing and pain relief. An uncontrolled 20-person laser/plasma series also reported wound closure, but none establishes eradication of bone infection.

Publications and records

4relevant publications

Publication and study types

Human RCT: 1 mapped osteomyelitis-associated diabetic-foot ulcer trial, ulcer-closure outcome

Human controlled non-randomized study: 1 jaw study (n=8)

Human uncontrolled case series: 1 (n=20; two representative cases detailed; laser plus plasma/PRP-based wound care)

Animal: 1 rat MRSA osteomyelitis model

No in-vitro study identified

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Osteomyelitis-associated diabetic-foot ulcers (n=20; randomized 10 per arm): >90% wound closure occurred in 7/10 active-treatment participants versus 1/10 sham participants (P=0.006). Percent wound-size reduction also favored active PBM (P=0.018). These are ulcer outcomes, not estimates of bone-infection clearance (Haze et al., 2022).

Jaw osteomyelitis after surgery (n=8; four per arm): clinical achievement was better with LED treatment at 3 and 6 months, and pain/discomfort resolution favored treatment. The abstract gives no numerical between-group estimates (Keković et al., 2023).

Combined-treatment series (n=20; uncontrolled): the report states that all patients achieved complete wound healing over about 4–6 months; two representative cases are described in detail. Laser was combined with a plasma/PRP-based intervention and standard wound care, so the outcome cannot be attributed to PBM (Sani and Sani, 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term wound closure in osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers

Low for postoperative jaw healing and pain

Very low for bone infection eradication

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small sham-controlled pilot found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated foot ulcers, and a very small jaw study reported better postoperative healing and pain relief. An uncontrolled 20-person laser/plasma series also reported wound closure, but none establishes eradication of bone infection.

Summary of the Evidence

Four unique publications were identified: one sham-controlled randomized pilot in people with osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers, one small controlled nonrandomized jaw study, one uncontrolled 20-patient diabetic-foot report with two representative cases described in detail, and one rat MRSA osteomyelitis experiment. The diabetic-foot reports are narrowly mapped from a wound category: the randomized trial measured ulcer closure, not eradication of bone infection, while the combined-treatment report cannot isolate PBM from plasma/PRP-based treatment and other wound care. No duplicate cohort was identified among these four publications.

Human and clinical evidence

In the sham-controlled pilot, 20 people with severe diabetic foot ulcers described as osteomyelitis-associated received standard care plus active or sham at-home PBM. Seven of ten active-treatment participants achieved more than 90% wound closure, compared with one of ten in the sham group. Wound-size reduction also favored PBM. These results concern closure of the associated ulcer; the trial did not establish microbiological or radiological clearance of osteomyelitis (Haze et al., 2022, PMID 34052927).

A prospective controlled study of eight people with secondary chronic osteomyelitis of the jaws compared standard postoperative care with or without PBM. The four treated patients had better clinical-achievement scores at three and six months, and pain and discomfort resolved more often. The groups were very small and allocation was not randomized (Keković et al., 2023, PMID 38405576).

An uncontrolled report describes 20 patients with osteomyelitis-associated diabetic-foot ulcers, with two representative cases presented in detail. The authors report complete wound healing in all 20 over about four to six months after laser plus a plasma-based intervention, antibiotics, and wound care; the abstract describes the plasma treatment as PRP. With no comparator and several co-interventions, the series cannot isolate PBM or establish bone-infection clearance (Sani and Sani, 2025, PMID 41305962).

Animal evidence

In a rat chronic osteomyelitis model caused by MRSA, debridement plus 808-nm near-infrared laser treatment was associated with dose-related reductions in histopathological infection compared with untreated controls. The experiment supports an antimicrobial or tissue-level effect in that specific model, not a clinical bone-infection cure (Kaya et al., 2011, PMID 21219239).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly testing PBM for osteomyelitis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The diabetic-foot pilot used daily pulsed 808-nm near-infrared light at 8.8 J/cm², applied directly to the wound at home for up to 12 weeks. The jaw study used an extraoral pulsed 635-nm red LED at 2.5 Hz for five sessions over two weeks. The rat study compared 808-nm near-infrared exposures of 7.64, 15.29, and 22.93 J/cm² after debridement. The 2025 series also reports 200-mW red light pulsed at 3000 Hz, with 6 J around wound margins and 4 J along vascular pathways, three laser sessions weekly plus two plasma sessions weekly. The routes, doses, co-interventions, and outcomes differ, and no common clinical dose has been established.

Interpretation

One small randomized pilot reported substantially greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers, and the jaw study reported better postoperative healing and pain outcomes. The rat experiment found dose-related improvement in infection histology. Human studies have not yet shown that PBM clears bone infection or prevents recurrence, so wound closure and pain should not be presented as infection eradication.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

A small sham-controlled trial found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated diabetic-foot ulcers, while a four-versus-four jaw study reported better healing and pain outcomes without extractable effect estimates. Neither study tested bone-infection clearance or recurrence. An uncontrolled 20-person laser/plasma wound-care series cannot isolate PBM from its co-interventions.
